facts.fact: The view-through rate formula is (Total Completed Views / Total Measurable Impressions) x 100.
facts.value: (Total Completed Views / Total Measurable Impressions) x 100
facts.quote: (Total Completed Views / Total Measurable Impressions) x 100 = View-Through Rate (VTR)

facts.fact: According to the page, view-through rate shows how many people saw an ad, did not click right away, but remembered the brand and looked it up later.
facts.quote: It shows you how many people saw your ad, didn’t click right away, but remembered your brand and looked you up later.

facts.fact: The page defines a completed view as someone watching an ad from start to finish.
facts.quote: A **completed view** is exactly what it sounds like, someone watched your ad from start to finish.

facts.fact: The page defines an impression as one instance of an ad being served on a screen, whether or not it was watched.
facts.quote: An **impression** is just one instance of your ad being served on a screen, whether it was watched or not.

facts.fact: The page defines video completion rate (VCR) as the percentage of people who started an ad and watched it to the end.
facts.quote: This metric tells you what percentage of people who started your ad watched it all the way to the end.

facts.fact: The page defines viewability as whether an ad was in a position where a human could see it.
facts.quote: It answers a simple but important question: Was your ad in a position where a human could see it?

facts.fact: The page states that view-through reporting connects an ad exposure with a later visit or purchase.
facts.quote: View-through reporting connects an ad exposure with a later visit or purchase.

facts.fact: The guide was published on January 22, 2026.
The page states that viewers give an ad less than three seconds before their attention wanders, so the opening must hook them quickly.
facts.quote: You have less than **three seconds** to hook a viewer before their mind (or their thumb) wanders.

facts.fact: The page states that ads in the 15-second range often see the best completion rates.
facts.quote: Ads in the **15-second** range often see the best completion rates because they deliver a punchy message

facts.fact: The page gives a 7-day attribution window as an example setting for a local restaurant.
facts.quote: A local restaurant, for instance, might go with a **7-day window**.

facts.fact: The page gives a 30-day attribution window as an example setting for a realtor, possibly longer.
facts.quote: They'd probably set a **30-day window**, maybe even longer.

facts.fact: According to the page, Adwave's smart data places ads on top-tier channels such as ESPN and Bravo.
facts.quote: It uses smart data to place your ad on top-tier channels like ESPN and Bravo

facts.fact: The page describes an attribution window as a timer that starts when a person sees an ad, and conversions occurring before it expires can be credited to that ad.
facts.quote: Think of it like a stopwatch that starts when someone sees your ad.

facts.fact: Adwave states that for streaming TV (CTV) campaigns, a view-through rate between 15% and 35% puts an advertiser in a great spot.
facts.quote: if you're hitting a VTR between **15% and 35%**, you're in a great spot.

facts.fact: Adwave states that there is no single universal good view-through rate, because it depends on industry and where the ads run.
facts.quote: There's no single magic number, as a "good" **view-through rate** really depends on your industry and where you're running your ads.

facts.fact: Adwave defines video completion rate (VCR) as the percentage of people who started an ad and watched it all the way to the end.
facts.quote: Of all the people who _started_ my ad, what percentage watched it all the way to the end?

facts.fact: Adwave defines view-through rate (VTR) as the number of people who finished an ad compared to the total number of impressions served.
facts.quote: It looks at everyone who _finished_ the ad compared to the total number of times it was served (**impressions**).
